content: Ileus, a common complication following abdominal surgery, is associated with increased hospital stays and other postoperative complications. The development of ileus is considered multifactorial, and various strategies have been explored to prevent it. Chewing gum has been proposed as a potential intervention to reduce postoperative ileus by promoting early recovery of gastrointestinal (GI) function through cephalo-vagal stimulation. However, no comprehensive review of this intervention in the context of abdominal surgery has been conducted. The primary objective of this review was to determine whether chewing gum after surgery accelerates the recovery of gastrointestinal function. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and ISI Web of Science, up to June 2014. Additional sources, such as reference lists of identified studies, systematic reviews, and clinical trial registries, were also examined. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared postoperative chewing gum use to a control group were included in the analysis. Data collection and quality assessment were performed independently by two authors using an adapted Cochrane risk of bias tool. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion. The overall quality of evidence for each outcome was evaluated using the GRADE framework. Studies were categorized into subgroups based on the type of surgery: colorectal surgery (CRS), cesarean section (CS), and other surgeries (OS). The effects of chewing gum on outcomes such as time to first flatus (TFF), time to bowel movement (TBM), length of hospital stay (LOHS), and time to bowel sounds (TBS) were analyzed using meta-analyses with a random-effects model. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the influence of study quality, methodological factors, and the use of Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) programs. Meta-regression was used to explore whether surgical site or risk of bias scores influenced the effect size of the intervention. A total of 81 studies involving 9,072 participants were included in the review. Many studies were assessed as having a high or unclear risk of bias. The analysis demonstrated that chewing gum significantly reduced TFF, with an overall reduction of 10.4 hours. Subgroup analyses showed reductions of 12.5 hours in CRS, 7.9 hours in CS, and 10.6 hours in OS. Chewing gum also significantly reduced TBM, with an overall reduction of 12.7 hours. Subgroup reductions were 18.1 hours in CRS, 9.1 hours in CS, and 12.3 hours in OS. Additionally, chewing gum slightly reduced LOHS, with an overall reduction of 0.7 days. Subgroup reductions were 1.0 day in CRS, 0.2 days in CS, and 0.8 days in OS. TBS was also slightly reduced, with an overall reduction of 5.0 hours. Subgroup reductions were 3.2 hours in CRS, 4.4 hours in CS, and 6.3 hours in OS. The largest effect sizes were observed in CRS, while the smallest were seen in CS. Significant heterogeneity was noted in most analyses, except for TBS in CRS. There was no significant difference in mortality, infection rates, or readmission rates between the chewing gum and control groups. Some studies reported reduced nausea, vomiting, and other complications in the chewing gum group. Chewing gum was generally well-tolerated by participants, and there was little difference in cost between the groups in the two studies that reported this outcome. Sensitivity analyses based on study quality and robustness of review estimates revealed no clinically significant differences in effect sizes. In ERAS studies, sensitivity analyses showed a smaller effect size for TFF, a larger effect size for TBM, and no difference in LOHS between groups. Meta-regression analyses indicated that the surgical site was associated with the extent of the effect size on LOHS across all surgical subgroups, as well as on TFF and TBM in the CS and CRS subgroups. There was no evidence that risk of bias scores influenced the effect size for any outcome, and neither variable explained the heterogeneity observed between studies. In conclusion, this review provides some evidence supporting the use of postoperative chewing gum to improve recovery of gastrointestinal function. However, the current body of research is limited, primarily focusing on CS and CRS, and consists largely of small, low-quality trials. Many components of the ERAS program also target ileus, potentially diminishing the additional benefit of chewing gum when used alongside ERAS, as observed in this review. Larger, high-quality RCTs conducted within an ERAS framework and across a broader range of surgical disciplines are needed to strengthen the evidence base for the use of chewing gum after surgery.
